# Theme ------------------------------------------------------------------------

    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1.1), face = "bold"),

# Toy data ---------------------------------------------------------------------
y <- c(6.1, 5.4, 7.2, 8.9, 9.1, 11.6)

x2 <- c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1)

toy_data <- tibble(y, x1, x2)

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, we should be able to:

- Read and write a regression model in matrix form,
  **and explain what each piece means**.
- Explain what the OLS estimator is *trying to do* before you see the formula.
- Derive the normal equations geometrically (no calculus needed) and with
  calculus.
- Estimate the error variance and the coefficient covariance matrix.
- Construct confidence and prediction intervals.
- Reproduce all of the above in R.

## The big picture

We already know how to fit a regression model

Today, we will express the same ideas using matrices

$$
\boxed{
\text{Model} \rightarrow \text{Predictions} \rightarrow \text{Residuals} \rightarrow \text{Minimise SSE}
}
$$

<br>

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
A matrix is just a tidy way of storing a table of numbers so we can do
**many calculations in one go**
:::

## Why use matrix notation

Let's suppose we have $n$ observations and $k$ predictors

For each observation $i = 1, \dots, n$ we can write

$$
Y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_kX_{ik} + \varepsilon_i
$$


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Writing this out **for every observation** is tedious

Matrices let us write all $n$ equations as **one** equation

The same formulas then work for 1 predictor or 100 predictors

:::

## A small example

Three observations, two predictors

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_1 &= \beta_0+\beta_1X_{11}+\beta_2X_{12}+\varepsilon_1,\\
Y_2 &= \beta_0+\beta_1X_{21}+\beta_2X_{22}+\varepsilon_2,\\
Y_3 &= \beta_0+\beta_1X_{31}+\beta_2X_{32}+\varepsilon_3
\end{aligned}
$$

<br>

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The coefficients $\beta$ are **the same** in every equation
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The predictor values $X$ and the errors $\varepsilon$ **change** from row to row
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
How could we **collect these equations** into a single expression?
:::

## The one matrix idea you need {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### Matrix times vector = a stack of "row $\times$ column" calculations

To multiply a matrix by a vector, take each **row** of the matrix, multiply it
entry-by-entry with the vector, and add

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 6 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} 1(10) + 4(2) \\ 1(10) + 5(2) \\ 1(10) + 6(2) \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} 18 \\ 20 \\ 22 \end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Each row of the answer is **one** observation's prediction

That is exactly what a regression model does: take each observation's
predictor values, multiply by the coefficients, and add

:::

## Matrix notation {style="font-size: 85%;"}

### The response vector

Let $\mathbf Y$ denote the [response vector]{.alert}
(i.e., a vector of observed responses)

$$
\mathbf{Y} = \begin{bmatrix}
Y_1 \\
Y_2 \\
\vdots \\
Y_n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

With dimension $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}$

Within this matrix there is one row for every observation and one
column containing the response.

## Matrix notation {style="font-size: 85%;"}

### The design matrix

Let $\mathbf{X}$ denote the [design matrix]{.alert} such that:

$$
\mathbf{X}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & X_{11} & \cdots &X_{1k} \\
1 & X_{21} & \cdots &X_{2k} \\
\vdots &\vdots &\ddots &\vdots \\
1 & X_{n1} & \cdots & X_{nk}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

- **Rows** = observations (row $i$ holds the predictor values for
  observation $i$)
- **Columns** = model terms (the first column of ones is for the intercept)
- There are $n$ rows and $p = k + 1$ columns, so
  $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
## Why a column of ones?

So that $\beta_0$ is multiplied by 1 in every row
:::

## Matrix notation {style="font-size: 85%;"}

### The parameter and error vectors

We can collect all the unknown parameters and errors into a
[parameter vector]{.alert} and an [error vector]{.alert}, respectively

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0 \\
\beta_1 \\
\vdots \\
\beta_k
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \begin{bmatrix}
\varepsilon_1 \\
\varepsilon_2 \\
\vdots \\
\varepsilon_n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::

::::

- $\boldsymbol\beta$ has $p = k + 1$ unknown **parameters** (one per
  column of $\mathbf X$)
- $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ has $n$ unknown **errors** (one per observation)

## Matrix notation {style="font-size: 85%;"}

### The matrix model

$$
\boxed{\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}
$$


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Written out for our three-observation, two-predictor example:

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ Y_3 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf Y\ (3 \times 1)}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & X_{11} & X_{12} \\
1 & X_{21} & X_{22} \\
1 & X_{31} & X_{32}
\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf X\ (3 \times 3)}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\beta\ (3 \times 1)}
+
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \varepsilon_3 \end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon\ (3 \times 1)}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Multiply the first row of $\mathbf X$ by $\boldsymbol\beta$ and we recover
$Y_1 = \beta_0+\beta_1X_{11}+\beta_2X_{12}+\varepsilon_1$

The single matrix equation **is** the three equations stacked together

:::

## Dimension check

Matrix multiplication only works when the [inner dimensions match]{.alert}

$$
\underbrace{\mathbf{X}}_{n \; \times \; p} \quad
\underbrace{\boldsymbol\beta}_{p \; \times \; 1} \quad = \quad
\underbrace{\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta}_{n \; \times \; 1}
$$

| Object | Dimension | Meaning |
|:--------------------|:-------------:|:--------------------------------|
| $\mathbf Y$ | $n \times 1$ | observed responses |
| $\mathbf X$ | $n \times p$ | predictor values (plus ones) |
| $\boldsymbol\beta$ | $p \times 1$ | true coefficients (unknown) |
| $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ | $n \times 1$ | true errors (unknown) |

<br>

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
## Habit to build: whenever you see a matrix formula, check the dimensions
:::

## Fitted values and residuals

We never see $\boldsymbol\beta$ or $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$, so we estimate them

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

[Fitted values]{.alert .center}

$$
\widehat{\mathbf Y} = \mathbf X \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
$$

What the model *predicts* for each observation

:::

::: {.column}

[Residuals]{.alert .center}

$$
\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{Y} - \widehat{\mathbf Y} = \mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
$$

What the model *got wrong* for each observation

:::
::::

<br>

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
## Our objective

Find the $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ that makes the residuals collectively
as small as possible in the **least-squares** sense
:::

## Ordinary least squares {style="font-size:85%;"}

### What are we minimising?

Using ordinary least squares we want to minimise

$$
S(\beta) = \sum^n_{j = 1}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1x_{i1} - \dots - \beta_kx_{ik})^2
$$

In matrix form we can represent this as

$$
S(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = (\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why does this work?

- $(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})$ is a **column vector** $(n \times 1)$
- Transposing it turns it into a **row vector** $(1 \times n)$
- Row $\times$ column gives a single number: $e_1^2 + e_2^2 + \dots + e_n^2$

In short: $\mathbf e^\mathsf T\mathbf e$ is the sum of squared residuals
:::

## Ordinary least squares

### Using calculus

If we expand out our above equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
S(\boldsymbol{\beta}) &= (\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}) \\[4pt]
&=\mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} -\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} + \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} \\[4pt]
&=\mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - \underbrace{\mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} -\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y}}_{\text{These two equations are the same}} + \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} \\[4pt]
&= \mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - 2 \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} +\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{S(\boldsymbol{\beta}) =  \mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - 2 \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} +\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}}
$$

::: {.notes}
- This is simply a matrix version of $(a - b)(a - b) = a^2 - 2ab + b^2$
:::

## Differentiate to minimise {style="font-size: 80%"}

$$
\boxed{S(\boldsymbol{\beta}) =  \mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - 2 \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} +\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}}
$$

When we differentiate the above equation with respect to $\beta$, we are left
with

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}} = -2\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} + 2 \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}
$$

Setting this equal to 0

$$
-2 \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} + 2\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X} \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = 0
$$


:::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Which can then be simplified down into

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$


::: {.callout-important}
## This is our normal equation
:::

::::

## Solving for $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$

To get a formula for estimating $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ we can multiply both
sides of our equation by the inverse of $\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}$
(the matrix version of dividing) such that

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$


<br>

::: {.callout-important}
## The formula requires $\mathbf X$ to have full column rank

This means no column is an exact linear combination of the others
:::

## What if the matrix is not invertible? {style="font-size:90%;"}

If the columns of $\mathbf{X}$ are linearly dependent, then
$\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}$ is singular and the usual inverse formula
does not apply

::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Common causes

- A predictor is an exact linear combination of other predictors
- Two columns are identical
- A categorical variable has an indicator for **every** category *and* the model has an intercept (the "dummy variable trap")
- Fewer observations than parameters ($n < p$)

Near-linear dependence is also a problem: the estimates become numerically
unstable
:::

## A small example

<br>

```{r}
#| label: small-data-plot
small_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "X", y = "Y") +
  theme_st303()
```

## A small example {style="font-size: 80%;"}

$$
Y = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \qquad
X = \begin{bmatrix} 1  & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Build the two pieces of the normal equations

$$
\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix} \qquad
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 23\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment}

Solve

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \widehat{\beta}_0 \\ \widehat{\beta}_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 23\end{bmatrix}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat{y} = 0.33 + 1.5x
$$

:::

## How noisy is the error? Estimating $\sigma^2$

We assume the errors have constant variance $\sigma^2$

We estimate it from the residuals

$$
\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\sum^n_{i = 1}e^2_i}{n - p} = \frac{\mathbf e^\mathsf T\mathbf e}{n - p}
$$


::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
We divide by $n - p$ (the **residual degrees of freedom**), not $n$, because
we used up $p$ pieces of information estimating $\boldsymbol\beta$
:::

## Representing our variance {style="font-size:80%;"}

### The covariance matrix

Under the model assumptions, $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is unbiased

$$
E(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
=\boldsymbol\beta
$$

and its (estimated) covariance matrix is

$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\widehat{\sigma}^2
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
}
$$

How to read it (a $p \times p$ table)

- **Diagonal** entries are the estimated variances of each coefficient
- Taking square roots gives the **standard errors**
- **Off-diagonal** entries are covariances between pairs of coefficients

## Making predictions from a model

For one observation

$$
\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta_0} + \hat{\beta_1}x_{i1} + \dots + \hat{\beta_k}x_{ik}
$$

For all observations at once

$$
\widehat{\mathbf Y} = \mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
$$


:::: {.fragment .fade-up}

For any **new** set of predictor values $\mathbf x_0$, the predicted mean response is

$$
\boxed{\widehat{y}_0 = \mathbf{x}_0^\mathsf{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
$$

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
$\mathbf x_0$ must contain the same model terms, in the same order, as the
columns of $\mathbf X$ (including the leading 1)
:::
::::

## Confidence interval for the mean response {style="font-size: 85%;"}

We want to estimate the **average** response at
$\mathbf{x}_0 = (1, x_{01}, \dots, x_{0k})^\mathsf{T}$

Our estimate is

$$
\widehat{\mu}_0 = \widehat{y}_0 = \mathbf x_0^\mathsf T \widehat{\boldsymbol \beta}
$$

with a standard error of

$$
SE_{\text{fit}}=
\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{
\mathbf x_0^\mathsf T
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf x_0
}
$$

A $100 (1 - \alpha)\%$ confidence interval is

$$
\boxed{\widehat y_0 \pm t_{n-p,\,1-\alpha/2}SE_{\text{fit}}}
$$

This quantifies uncertainty about the **conditional mean** at those
predictor values

## Prediction interval for a new observation {style="font-size: 85%;"}

For a single **new** observation at $\mathbf{x}_0$, the estimate is the same

$$
\widehat{y}_0 = \mathbf x_0^\mathsf T \widehat{\boldsymbol \beta}
$$

but the standard error includes the extra noise of an individual outcome

$$
SE_{\text{pred}}=
\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{
\textcolor{blue}{1}+
\mathbf x_0^\mathsf T
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf x_0
}
$$

Thus, a $100 (1 - \alpha)\%$ prediction interval is

$$
\boxed{\widehat y_0 \pm t_{n-p,\,1-\alpha/2}SE_{\text{pred}}}
$$

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
The extra $1$ is the new observation's own error $\varepsilon_0$, so prediction
intervals are always **wider** than confidence intervals
:::

## Simple linear regression (using matrices)

Consider the simple linear regression model

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_i + \varepsilon_i
$$

The design matrix can be written as

$$
\mathbf X= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & X_1 \\ 1 & X_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & X_n \end{bmatrix}
$$


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

The ordinary least squares estimator is

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
$$


:::

## Simple linear regression (using matrices) {style="font-size: 70%;"}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="33%"}

$$
\mathbf X= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & X_1 \\ 1 & X_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & X_n \end{bmatrix}
$$

::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}

<br>

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf T= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ X_1 & X_2 & \cdots & X_n \end{bmatrix}
$$

::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}


::: {.fragment}

<br>

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X= \begin{bmatrix}
n & \sum X_i \\
\sum X_i & \sum X_i^2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::
::::
:::::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix

$$
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1} =
\frac{1}{\text{det}(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)} \begin{bmatrix}
\sum X_i^2 & -\sum X_i \\
-\sum X_i & n
\end{bmatrix} \qquad \text{ where det}(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X) = n\sum X_i^2-\left(\sum X_i\right)^2 = nS_{xx}
$$

:::


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum Y_i\\
\sum X_iY_i
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::



::::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Multiplying the matrices and simplifying gives the formulas you already know

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\boxed{\widehat\beta_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
\boxed{\widehat\beta_0 = \bar Y - \widehat \beta_1 \bar X}
$$

:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Matrix notation generalises the least-squares procedure
:::

:::::

## The coefficient covariance matrix in simple linear regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

Recall that

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\sigma^2(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1} =
\frac{1}{\text{det}(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)} \begin{bmatrix}
\sum X_i^2 & -\sum X_i \\[4pt]
-\sum X_i & n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::
::::

Thus

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2 \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\sum X_i^2}{nS_{xx}} & - \frac{\sum X_i}{nS_{xx}} \\[4pt]
-\frac{\sum X_i}{nS_{xx}} & \frac{n}{nS_{xx}}
\end{bmatrix}
$$


::::: {.fragment .fade-up}


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_0)
=\sigma^2\left(
\frac1n+\frac{\bar X^2}{S_{xx}}
\right)
$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_1)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}
$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat\beta_1)
=-\frac{\bar X\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}
$$

:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
The matrix expression gives the variances and covariance of the two coefficient
estimates in one calculation.
:::

:::::

## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

Suppose we observe six responses and two predictors

We want to fit

$$
Y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \beta_2X_{i1}^2 + \beta_3X_{i2} +\varepsilon_i
$$


```{r}
#| label: matrix-data

toy_data |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```


## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### Constructing the design matrix

The columns must correspond to the model terms in the order

$$
(1,\ X_1,\ X_1^2,\ X_2)
$$

```{r}
#| label: design-matrix
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

X <- model.matrix(~ x1 + I(x1^2) + x2, data = toy_data)

X

# Check the dimensions: n x p
n <- nrow(X)
p <- ncol(X)
c(n = n, p = p)
```

## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### Calculate the OLS estimates

$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$

```{r}
#| label: estimate-coefficients
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

# Create the response vector
Y <- matrix(y, ncol = 1)

# Calculate XtX
XtX <- crossprod(X)

# Calculate XtY
XtY <- crossprod(X, Y)

# Calcuate the OLS estimates for the betas
beta_hats <- solve(XtX, XtY)

beta_hats
```


## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### Verifying our answers

```{r}
#| label: verify-model
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
fit <- lm(y ~ x1 + I(x1^2) + x2, data = toy_data)

summary(fit)
```


## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Calculate fitted values and residuals

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

[**Fitted values**]{.center}

$$
\widehat{\mathbf Y} = \mathbf X \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

[**Residuals**]{.center}

$$
\mathbf e=\mathbf Y-\widehat{\mathbf Y}
$$

:::
::::

```{r}
#| label: fitted-residuals
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

y_hat <- X %*% beta_hats
e <- Y - y_hat

tibble(
  observed = y,
  fitted = drop(y_hat),
  residual = drop(e)
)
```

## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### Estimate $\sigma^2$ and the covariance matrix

$$
\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\mathbf e^\mathsf T\mathbf e}{n-p}
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \widehat{\sigma}^2(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
$$

```{r}
#| label: covariance
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

sigma2_hat <- drop(crossprod(e) / (n - p))
XtX_inv <- solve(XtX)

var_beta <- sigma2_hat * XtX_inv
var_beta

# Standard errors: square roots of the diagonal
sqrt(diag(var_beta))
```

## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 85%;"}

### Confidence and prediction intervals

Predict at $X_1 = 2$ and $X_2 = 1$, so $\mathbf x_0^\mathsf T = (1,\ 2,\ 2^2,\ 1)$

```{r}
#| label: intervals
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

new_data <- tibble(x1 = 2, x2 = 1)

# Row vector x0' (1 x p), with terms in the same order as X
x0 <- model.matrix(~ x1 + I(x1^2) + x2, data = new_data)

y0_hat <- drop(x0 %*% beta_hats)

# Standard errors
q <- drop(x0 %*% XtX_inv %*% t(x0))
se_fit <- sqrt(sigma2_hat * q)
se_pred <- sqrt(sigma2_hat * (1 + q))

t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n - p)

tibble(
  fit = y0_hat,
  ci_lower = y0_hat - t_crit * se_fit,
  ci_upper = y0_hat + t_crit * se_fit,
  pi_lower = y0_hat - t_crit * se_pred,
  pi_upper = y0_hat + t_crit * se_pred
)
```

## Summary {style="font-size: 75%;"}

The multiple regression model can be expressed as

$$
\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+
\boldsymbol\varepsilon
$$

The OLS estimator is

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
$$

when $\mathbf X$ has full column rank

The residuals satisfy

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf e= 0
$$

The estimated coefficient covariance matrix is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\widehat\sigma^2
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
$$

These expressions underpin coefficient estimation, uncertainty quantification,
confidence intervals and prediction intervals.
